intro: The Safety Framework sets out the integrated system of principles, practices, and responsibilities that guide how safety is planned, managed, and continuously improved across all sport activities and operations. It is informed by the ISO 31000 Risk Management principles and the ISO 45001 Occupational Health and Safety Management System standards.

standards.name: ISO 31000 — Risk Management
standards.body: Provides principles and guidelines for risk management applicable across any organisation. The Framework draws on ISO 31000 to ensure that risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring are embedded systematically into all sport safety planning and operations.

standards.name: ISO 45001 — Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems
standards.body: Specifies requirements for an occupational health and safety (OHS) management system. The Framework aligns with ISO 45001 to support the organisation in providing safe and healthy workplaces, preventing work-related injury and illness, and proactively improving OHS performance.

domains.name: Sport Safety
domains.body: Covers the safety of athletes, participants, coaches, officials, and spectators across all sport programmes, facilities, and events — including physical hazards, environmental risks, equipment standards, and emergency preparedness.

domains.name: Safe Sport
domains.body: Addresses safeguarding, athlete welfare, and protection from abuse, harassment, and exploitation in sport. Ensures that all individuals can participate in an environment that is safe, fair, and free from harm.

domains.name: Workplace Safety
domains.body: Covers the occupational health and safety of staff, volunteers, contractors, and other workers involved in sport delivery — aligned to the Workplace Safety and Health Act and ISO 45001 requirements.

drivers.name: Commitment
drivers.body: Leadership commitment is the foundation of effective safety management. Boards, executives, and managers visibly champion safety, allocate adequate resources, and hold themselves accountable for outcomes.
elements: Safety as a standing agenda item

drivers.name: Culture
drivers.body: A strong safety culture exists when every individual internalises safety as a shared value rather than a compliance obligation — built through open reporting, consistent behaviour, and learning from incidents.

drivers.name: Competencies
drivers.body: Safe sport delivery depends on people having the knowledge, skills, and judgement to identify hazards, apply controls, and respond to emergencies — built through structured training and credentialing.
elements: Mandatory certifications for coaches and instructors

drivers.name: Controls
drivers.body: Controls are the physical, procedural, and administrative measures that reduce the likelihood and severity of harm, applied through the hierarchy of controls — eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, protect.

drivers.name: Collaboration
drivers.body: No single person or team owns safety. Collaboration means partners, contractors, national sport associations, and facility operators work together through shared standards, joint planning, and mutual accountability.

drivers.name: Communication
drivers.body: Safety information must reach the right people at the right time — from pre-event briefings and hazard signage to incident reporting channels and the feedback loop that closes action taken.

enablers.name: Leadership & Governance
enablers.body: The board and executive layer sets safety direction, approves policy, and monitors performance through defined governance structures and reporting lines.

enablers.name: Policy & Strategy
enablers.body: Policies translate governance intent into binding requirements. Strategy sets the multi-year direction for safety improvement aligned to the organisation's vision.

enablers.name: Innovation & Technology
enablers.body: Technology and data are leveraged to improve hazard detection, incident reporting, training delivery, and safety performance monitoring.

enablers.name: Competence & Capability
enablers.body: Building the human capital needed to deliver safe sport — through training pipelines, credentialing schemes, and succession planning for safety-critical roles.

enablers.name: Risk Management
enablers.body: Systematic identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring of risks across all sport programmes, events, and facilities — aligned to ISO 31000 principles.

enablers.name: Planning & Assurance
enablers.body: Operational safety plans, audit programmes, and assurance reviews that verify controls are in place and effective.

enablers.name: Performance & Improvement
enablers.body: Tracking safety KPIs, learning from incidents, and driving continuous improvement across the organisation.

enablers.name: Information & Intelligence
enablers.body: Collecting and analysing safety data — incidents, near-misses, audits, and benchmarks — to generate actionable insights.

enablers.name: Operational Management
enablers.body: Day-to-day safety management of facilities, programmes, and events — the operational layer where policy and strategy are put into practice.

environment.name: Strategic Vision
environment.body: The long-term vision that shapes the organisation's safety ambition and direction.

environment.name: Organisational Context
environment.body: The internal and external factors — structure, culture, resources, and relationships — within which the safety management system operates.

environment.name: Scope and Boundaries
environment.body: The defined boundaries of the safety management system: which activities, facilities, people, and operations it covers.

environment.name: Stakeholder Expectations
environment.body: Understanding and responding to the safety expectations of athletes, participants, partners, regulators, and the public.

environment.name: Duty of Care
environment.body: The legal and ethical responsibility shared by all who deliver or host sport to take reasonable steps to prevent foreseeable harm.

environment.name: Legal and Statutory Obligations
environment.body: Compliance with the Workplace Safety and Health Act, sport-specific statutory requirements, and applicable codes of practice and regulations.
